      <news:title><![CDATA[From Microsoft, US bank outages to European freezer hack, why are cyber attackers not getting caught?]]></news:title>
      <news:keywords><![CDATA[initially said there was no evidence of malicious activity behind the disruption. A few days later, the company warned users about threat actors exploiting the situation by circulating fake outage-related emails. These messages were designed to take advantage of the disruption and potentially trick users into engaging with malicious content. While the two developments do not necessarily contradict each other, they highlight how difficult it can be to separate an actual technical failure from malicious activity taking advantage of it. Microsoft is not the only company facing questions over unexplained disruptions. US banks have also experienced service outages and transaction delays, with customers left looking for answers. In JPMorgan Chase's case, the bank attributed the November 16 disruption to a software issue in its hardware systems and said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Meanwhile, Europe has been dealing with a different kind of cyber incident. In October, hundreds of French supermarkets reportedly suffered attacks targeting their refrigeration systems, forcing businesses to discard food and absorb substantial financial losses. The French government blamed it on an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) unit, Shahid Kaveh, as responsible for attacks on approximately 700 grocery stores and other retail sites on October 11 and 12, according to Axios. French intelligence said hackers manipulated refrigeration controls, pushing freezer temperatures beyond safe levels and causing losses worth tens of millions of euros. Iran has denied the allegations. Cyber attacks on supermarket freezers were reported from at least nine European countries including Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Portugal and the UK. Nowhere investigators could conclusively find the people or groups behind the hacking that caused huge economic and business losses to these countries. In the UK, where food suppliers reported attacks on refrigeration systems, its National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said it is working with affected businesses, although the disruption so far has been limited. These incidents point to a larger problem. When systems go down, businesses are not always able to establish whether they are dealing with a cyberattack, a software failure or an infrastructure problem. Even when malicious activity is suspected, identifying the people or groups behind it can be another challenge altogether. Has AI made it easier for attackers to conceal their identities? Are increasingly interconnected systems making it harder to trace the source of disruptions? And what happens when organisations cannot establish the cause of an outage quickly enough? To understand these questions, we spoke to cybersecurity experts about why attribution is becoming increasingly complicated, how companies can investigate disruptions and what businesses need to do to prevent similar incidents. Why are outages becoming harder to explain, even when several organisations are affected? One of the biggest challenges with modern digital infrastructure is that a disruption in one system can affect several others. This means that multiple organisations experiencing problems around the same time does not automatically point towards a coordinated cyberattack. Padma Reddy Sama, CTO and co-founder of BharathCloud, said technological disruptions can stem from several causes, including software issues, configuration errors, hardware faults, network failures and failures in interconnected systems. Explaining the November 16 banking disruption, he said JPMorgan Chase’s transaction delays have been linked to a software issue in its hardware systems. The firm found no evidence of a cyberattack. The bank also clarified that delays experienced by other banks could have originated from their dependence on Chase rather than failures within their own infrastructure. "The technology issue is that it is interconnected. A break in any one system has a ripple effect on all the other systems that use it, be it applications, payments or partner systems. In relation to banking, this could mean delays to transactions and disruptions to customer services, without impacting customers' money or access," Reddy said. The financial consequences, however, can extend well beyond the immediate disruption. Citing IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report, Reddy pointed out that the average cost of a data breach in India has reached Rs 25.5 crore, marking a 15.9 per cent increase from 2025. He said organisations need to prioritise resilient infrastructure, continuous monitoring, backups and disaster recovery mechanisms. Restoring services is only one part of the process; businesses must also ensure that an initial failure does not develop into a larger crisis. Ritwik Batabyal, CTO and Innovation Officer at Mastek, believes the growing complexity of digital infrastructure is making it difficult to understand the full picture when something goes wrong. "The paradox of modern technology is that systems have become more observable individually, but less understandable collectively. A small failure in one deeply interconnected component can create symptoms across dozens of organisations, making the blast radius look much larger than the actual fault," he said. Batabyal said the JPMorgan incident illustrates why simultaneous disruptions should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of a common attack. "The larger lesson is: simultaneous disruption does not necessarily mean a common attack; interconnectedness itself can amplify failure," he said. How can companies establish whether an outage was caused by a cyberattack? Identifying the cause of an outage requires more than looking at when a system stopped functioning. Organisations need to reconstruct what happened before, during and after the disruption, while examining evidence across their entire infrastructure. According to Reddy, companies must rely on structured incident investigations rather than assumptions. This involves examining system logs, network traffic, access records, authentication requests and infrastructure changes around the time of the incident. Security teams then need to correlate this information across applications, servers, cloud platforms and third-party services to understand where the failure originated. There are also important differences between a technical malfunction and a possible cyberattack. Software bugs, misconfigurations and capacity problems can trigger outages, while suspicious login attempts, unauthorised access, data exfiltration and privilege escalation could indicate malicious activity. However, no single indicator is necessarily proof of an attack. Investigators need to examine the evidence collectively before reaching a conclusion. Reddy also referred to Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, which identified software exploitation as accounting for approximately 31 per cent of intrusion vectors. He said this reinforces the importance of vulnerability management, regular software updates and stronger access controls. Organisations should also maintain centralised monitoring and immutable logs to preserve evidence during an incident. Where necessary, external cybersecurity specialists and digital forensic investigators can help establish the root cause. Batabyal said companies need to rethink how they monitor their systems. "We need to move from monitoring uptime to reconstructing causality. Organisations need end-to-end telemetry across identity, network, application, infrastructure and third-party dependencies so they can reconstruct the digital chain of events," he said. In other words, knowing that a system failed is no longer enough. Companies must also have the information needed to establish why it failed and what happened along the way. "So we should not just observe that the system failed; we should preserve enough evidence to explain why it failed. That is becoming as important as disaster recovery itself," Batabyal said. French supermarket attacks show cyber risks are no longer limited to digital systems The attacks on French supermarkets offer another example of how cybercriminals can cause damage without necessarily stealing customer information or compromising conventional IT systems. Instead of targeting databases or payment information, the attackers reportedly manipulated refrigeration controls, affecting the physical operations of grocery stores. Reddy said the incident demonstrates how cyberattacks have expanded beyond traditional IT infrastructure into operational technology (OT), which controls physical equipment such as refrigeration units, power systems and industrial machinery. He explained that identifying those responsible requires detailed forensic investigations involving access logs, IP addresses, remote sessions, connected devices, network traffic and system modifications. For businesses, the immediate priority should be to understand which devices are connected to their networks, restrict unnecessary remote access, apply security patches and closely monitor third-party systems. The incident also highlights why seemingly ordinary business equipment cannot be overlooked when organisations assess their cybersecurity risks. Batabyal said the supermarket attacks demonstrate how digital vulnerabilities can translate directly into physical and financial damage. "The refrigerator incident demonstrates a fascinating inversion: cyber risk no longer needs to steal data to create economic damage—it can manipulate the physical world. Connected refrigeration systems were reportedly exposed through legacy technology, known vulnerabilities and weak/default credentials," he said. But establishing who carried out such attacks is considerably more complicated. Attackers can route their activities through compromised infrastructure spread across different countries, making it difficult for investigators to trace the original source. Batabyal believes organisations should look beyond identifying the attacker and examine why their systems allowed an external instruction to change physical operating conditions in the first place. "The bigger priority, therefore, is not simply 'Who attacked us?' but 'Why could an internet-originated instruction alter a physical operating parameter without sufficient verification?'" he said. He said cybersecurity frameworks must evolve to protect physical operations as well as digital information. "That is where the next frontier of cybersecurity lies: zero-trust must extend from data access to physical actions." The common thread across these incidents is that identifying an outage and establishing responsibility for it are two very different challenges. A service disruption may originate from a software bug, a compromised third-party system or a deliberate attack. Even when investigators establish that malicious activity took place, tracing it back to a particular group requires a separate layer of evidence. AI could add another dimension to this problem by changing how quickly attackers operate and how they use compromised infrastructure. However, the incidents discussed here do not establish that AI was responsible for concealing the attackers or causing the disruptions. For businesses, the bigger concern is the growing dependence on interconnected systems, where a failure in one component can quickly affect operations elsewhere. As the French supermarket attacks demonstrate, the consequences can extend beyond inaccessible websites or delayed transactions to physical goods, supply chains and substantial financial losses. The challenge for cybersecurity teams, therefore, is no longer simply preventing attacks. It is ensuring that when something goes wrong, they have enough evidence to understand what happened, contain the damage and establish accountability.
